links.claim: XLS-70 Credentials record an issuer's attestation about a subject account; the issuer defines what the credential means. They can support authorization checks, but the ledger does not conduct the underlying identity investigation. An accepted credential from a trusted issuer is different from an arbitrary account asserting that it passed KYC. [1] [2]

links.claim: The specification defines creating, accepting and deleting credentials and extends Deposit Authorization to accept credentials. The concept documentation distinguishes issuers, authorizers and users. An authorizer chooses the issuers and credential types it accepts. That choice is a trust policy, not an automatic consequence of a credential being stored on the ledger. [1] [2]

sources.title: XRPL Credentials: writer trust, article accuracy and identity evidence
sources.body:
XRPL Credentials attest to writer identity under an operator-trusted issuer. The writer accepts the credential, and the engine checks acceptance, expiration and issuer policy against validated Testnet evidence. A Credential does not prove an article is accurate. It does not increase the writer trust weight or change the price or spending policy.

Identity is not truth. A credential attests to a seller wallet, not an article, claim, reputation score or investment recommendation. Issuer trust is operator policy. Purchase decisions, trust weights, prices, budgets and payment authority are unchanged: only deterministic policy code can spend. Testnet only; no real value.

A refund after successful key publication is a separate writer-signed Payment. The ledger does not decide whether prose is useful, truthful or worth its price. A signed passage promise and a verifiable fraud proof establish responsibility for a broken commitment, but a real writer could refuse a refund. The fixture writer cooperates in our demonstrations. This limitation belongs beside the transaction evidence so that a reader does not mistake a cooperative recovery for unilateral buyer protection.

A writer no-show follows a different path. CancelAfter permits cancellation after the ledger deadline; it does not automatically return principal. Policy must submit EscrowCancel and observe a validated successful transaction before reporting principal returned. Fees remain spent. This is why a cancelled purchase and a refunded completed sale need separate labels and separate accounting. A pending reservation remains exposure until recovery proves the terminal state.

One charge per intent depends on durable state, rather than a retry counter in the user interface. The engine persists the signed transaction blob before submission and reuses the same obligation during recovery. It must not manufacture another principal purchase merely because a response was lost. The authorized budget remains the spending boundary across retries, replacements and refunds. Refunds do not replenish gross spending authorization.

Independent verification checks several different things. Offline cryptographic checks can authenticate the signed manifest, exact passage hashes, delivered identity and key binding. A ledger lookup separately establishes successful validated settlement. Historical endpoints can disagree about availability; a transaction not found on one endpoint is not proof of failure. Readers should retain the transaction hash, network, ledger index and receipt bundle when reporting evidence.

Faucet funds and public Testnet endpoints are suitable for reproducing this prototype without real money. Wallet seeds stay in private local storage and never enter model prompts, article text, receipts or public logs. Testnet balances have no real value. The displayed application prices do not imply a redeemable SGD balance or a guaranteed conversion into XRP. Network availability and faucet funding time remain operational dependencies.

The purchase receipt is an evidence bundle, not a quality endorsement. Readers should resolve each citation to the delivered passage, check that its exact text appears in the authenticated body, and keep the associated grant and settlement identifiers. Public search abstracts help decide what to investigate; they cannot substitute for paid evidence. A signed promise describes what a writer offers, whereas the delivered passage establishes what the buyer may actually cite. These boundaries apply equally to our own notes and to outside writers.

sources.title: What do XLS-70 Credentials attest to?
sources.body:
XLS-70 Credentials record an issuer's attestation about a subject account; the issuer defines what the credential means. They can support authorization checks, but the ledger does not conduct the underlying identity investigation. An accepted credential from a trusted issuer is different from an arbitrary account asserting that it passed KYC. [1] [2]

The specification defines creating, accepting and deleting credentials and extends Deposit Authorization to accept credentials. The concept documentation distinguishes issuers, authorizers and users. An authorizer chooses the issuers and credential types it accepts. That choice is a trust policy, not an automatic consequence of a credential being stored on the ledger. [1] [2]

I recommend validating the exact issuer, credential type, subject, acceptance and expiry before using a credential as an access signal. Do not promote all credential holders into verified experts. Expertise, identity and payment authorization ask different questions. Where underlying checks contain personal data, keep a clear boundary between the public attestation and the private evidence used by its issuer. [1] [2]

Exercise a matching credential, an untrusted issuer using the same type string, an unaccepted credential and expiration. Record the verifier's accepted-issuer policy with the result so another reviewer can reproduce it. These checks are recommendations based on XLS-70 and the concept documentation. They do not imply that credential issuance transfers statutory compliance responsibility from the service operator to a validator or guarantees continuing legal eligibility. [1] [2]

sources.title: Do Credentials replace KYC and AML controls?
sources.body:
On-ledger Credentials can carry attestations, but they do not replace the underlying customer due diligence and AML controls required of an in-scope service provider. The issuer defines the credential's meaning. A verifier must decide whether that issuer and assertion satisfy the purpose for which access is being granted. [1] [2]

MAS Notice PSN02 describes AML/CFT requirements for digital payment token service providers, including customer due diligence, record keeping and suspicious-transaction controls. The existence of a reusable attestation does not itself demonstrate that those operational duties have been performed. Identity evidence and ongoing transaction monitoring concern different parts of a service's risk management. [1] [2]

My recommendation is to document the trust contract behind each accepted credential: who investigated the customer, what was checked, how expiry and deletion are handled, and what the relying service still does itself. Keep sensitive supporting evidence outside public transaction fields. A credential type string should not become an unrestricted permission for any future activity or jurisdiction. [1] [2]

Test an expired assertion, an issuer no longer accepted by policy and a valid credential attached to an unrelated account. Review monitoring and record-retention behavior separately from that access test. These recommendations are derived from the Credentials roles and the MAS notice summary. They do not claim that any credential scheme automatically meets statutory reliance requirements or that the ledger performs sanctions screening for its users. [1] [2]
